body.text: Widow spends lifetime calling for gambling reforms after husband's suicide death in 1987
Janina Anstee's late husband, Leslie Anstee, began placing bets with bookmakers at 13 years old.
She estimates he gambled "hundreds of thousands" dollars away in his lifetime.
Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide.
Two weeks before Christmas in 1987, the 53-year-old died by suicide, overwhelmed by debt acquired from gambling.
Mr Anstee had been expected to attend his 15-year-old daughter's school concert but never made it.
"He promised her he would," Ms Anstee said.
"In those days, it was different. You had no mobile phone … he didn't ring me."
The next morning, she received a call from the police that he had been found dead.
At the time of his death, gambling had consumed the family's finances, leaving a debt of more than $30,000.
The 'thrill of the game'
It was a whirlwind romance between the pair.
At 19, Ms Anstee moved from Brisbane to the Gold Coast to pursue singing.
She began performing with a band at a local hotel.
"Unbeknownst to me, my husband was there. He was working as a head waiter," Ms Anstee said.
Mr Anstee convinced the hotel manager's son to hire her as a full-time singer.
She still remembers the first time he took her out for coffee.
"He told me all about his life," Ms Anstee said.
"Everything except the gambling."
Four years later, they married a week before Christmas in 1970.
By then the pair had moved to Sydney and went on to have three children.
The now-80-year-old still wears all her rings, including the one Mr Anstee bought even before they were engaged.
"He was very down to earth, very open, but had all these Aussie sayings … and they'd rhyme and everything," she said.
"He would have made a terrific comedian."
During their marriage, she was unaware of all the different techniques her husband used to acquire money for gambling, such as taking out different loans.
"[Gamblers] make bad decisions, and they think they can fix it up with gambling," Ms Anstee said.
She believes the "thrill of the game" kept him hooked, but she never saw him break down when he lost. She said a telling sign was him spending time with the birds in their backyard.
"I'd see the depression," she said.
Lifetime of advocacy
Following his death, Ms Anstee has been using her grief to advocate for gambling reforms.
"I don't want any other family to suffer as we have done," she said in a Woman's Day article in 1988.
"Our life was a nightmare as Les became lost in a web of lies and deceit … gambling became the centre of his world," she told a journalist less than a year after his death.
In the article, Ms Anstee laid out a seven-point plan to curb "a compulsive scourge" in gambling.

That included a ban on gambling advertising, a government committee to control gambling, educational programs in primary school and tighter credit controls for people with proven financial difficulties.

Alliance for Gambling Reform said those demands "closely mirror" many of the 31 recommendations of the You Win Some, You Lose More report into online gambling harm and its impacts on those experiencing gambling harm.
"Janina was making the case for reform 35 years before Parliament caught up," the alliance chair, Angela Tillmanns, said in August when awarding Ms Anstee its inaugural Lifetime Achievement award.
In 2023, a landmark report from a federal parliamentary inquiry led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy was released.

The report called for a ban on all online gambling advertising, national regulation and a national online gambling regulator, national campaigns targeting children and young people, and minimum gambling consumer protection standards to be implemented by banks.
Ms Anstee remembers seeing her plan for the first time alongside the report and feeling "over the moon" that someone else had the same ideas.
"I thought … wow," she told the ABC.
More than 1,000 days later, the federal government formally responded to the report.

In August this year, the federal parliament passed gambling reforms that the Labor government described as the "strongest ever" and "historic", aiming to reduce wagering advertising across television, radio and online and minimise children's exposure to gambling ads.
The changes take place from January.
"The government has listened to parents, to sports fans, to gambling harm reduction advocates, to broadcasters, to charities and to industry," Communication Minister Anika Wells said in August.
The Australian Gambling Research Centre data revealed that around three million Australians engaged in some form of harmful gambling in 2025.
"It's as bad, if not worse than, the drug problem," Ms Anstee said.
In almost four decades of advocacy, the now-grandmother said she would continue campaigning for change so other families don't experience the same hurt.
